table.brief: Row headers much longer than the one-line numeric data cells (e.g. "Net revenue retention, trailing twelve months")

understanding.purpose: Track six operating and financial metrics across FY 2022–FY 2024 and Q1 2025 so readers can assess trends and current performance.
understanding.reading: Readers identify the metric in the row header, then scan the four period columns left to right. Comparison happens horizontally within each row and vertically across metrics, so both row-label readability and period alignment matter.
groups: FY 2022, FY 2023 and FY 2024 form a historical annual series and should share a consistent width and rhythm.
Q1 2025 is the latest/current period; it belongs with the other periods but can be treated as a distinct endpoint.
The Metric column has a separate row-label role and needs enough width to keep labels scannable.
keep_intact: Period headers FY 2022, FY 2023, FY 2024 and Q1 2025 on one line where possible.
No breaking of currency amounts, percentages or identifiers.
may_wrap: Long Metric labels at word boundaries, especially 'Sales and marketing expense as a percentage of revenue', 'Net revenue retention, trailing twelve months', 'Customer acquisition cost, blended', 'Annual recurring revenue, end of period' and 'Free cash flow, trailing twelve months'.

preferred.name: r1A
preferred.note: Size each period column to the exact one-line requirement of its own widest header (FY 2022 88, FY 2023 90, FY 2024 89, Q1 2025 91) and give every remaining pixel to the Metric column (177px text). Fixes r0A's wrapped FY 2024 header without spending width the numbers don't need.

acceptable.name: r0A
acceptable.note: Maximize the row-label column while holding each period column at the minimum width that keeps its header and values intact.

acceptable.name: r0B
acceptable.note: Balance label readability with an even, rhythmic set of four equal period columns for easy horizontal comparison.

bad.name: r0C
bad.note: Prioritize generous period columns and comparison rhythm, accepting more wrapping in the metric labels.
bad.why: The metric column is starved to 156px while each numeric column gets 100px, forcing labels to five lines and rows up to 145px; the table becomes 645px tall with large empty numeric cells.

bad.name: r1B
bad.note: Uniform 90px period columns so the annual series and the current quarter share one identical rhythm and all headers fit on one line; Metric keeps 175px of text, enough to hold the longest label at three lines and keep rows reading as units.
bad.why: Splits the monetary value $548.2M into “$548.2” and “M” in the Q1 2025 column, so a number no longer reads as one atomic value.

bad.name: r1C
bad.note: Gives Q1 2025 a visibly wider column than the annual columns, marking it as the current endpoint of the series while keeping all headers single-line; Metric still gets 171px text, so no row exceeds three lines and the table stays short.
bad.why: Splits the monetary value $402.7M into “$402.7” and “M” in the FY 2023 column; currency amounts must not break mid-token.

rationale: r1A is the best balance: every year header and every value stays on one line, and the numeric columns sit at their minimum safe widths, leaving the remaining width to the metric labels. r0A is more compact and gives the metric column slightly better line breaks, but it wraps “FY 2024”, so the year-header row loses consistency. r0B is clean but unnecessarily tall, while r0C over-allocates width to short numbers and compresses the labels into five lines. r1B and r1C are disqualified because they split monetary values mid-token.

general: Allocate numeric columns by the widest header or value they must contain, not by equal width or symmetry; give the remainder to the descriptive row-header column.
Headers in a comparison series such as years should share one line and a common baseline; wrapping one header breaks scanning and makes the header row look arbitrary.
Never break numbers, currency amounts, or identifiers across lines; a mid-token split is worse than a slightly taller table.
A compact table is not automatically better: excessive numeric whitespace plus cramped labels is a proportion fault, not neutral space.
Row height is driven by the longest label in the row-header column; small width changes near a line-break threshold can change the whole table’s rhythm.
specific: Here the numeric columns need at least 88/90/89/91px to keep FY 2022, FY 2023, FY 2024, Q1 2025 and the longest values intact; the metric column then takes the remaining ~198px.
The critical threshold is only 4px: at 85px “FY 2024” wraps, while at 89px it fits; at 198px the metric labels wrap more than at 202px.
The row headers are long (up to 452px on one line), so the metric column dominates layout; numeric values are short and should not be given extra width.

tradeoffs: The main tradeoff is r0A’s 53px-shorter table versus its wrapped FY 2024 header; a designer with tight vertical space could accept the wrap. There is also a choice between equal numeric columns (r0B) and fitted numeric columns (r1A/r0A): equal widths look calmer but spend space on columns that do not need it. Widening numbers to look generous only steals width from labels and increases label wrapping.
uncertain: Whether one wrapped year header is acceptable enough to prefer r0A over r1A; the exact metric-column width at which the first row drops from three lines to two; and whether r0C is merely inefficient or clearly bad. Some designers might tolerate r1B/r1C’s single split as a minor wrap, but I would not.

critique.good: Best of the three. The wide Metric column (202px) keeps most labels to two lines, so rows read as units and the table stays compact at 461px. Numbers sit close to their labels, supporting left-to-right scanning.
critique.problems: The FY 2024 header wraps to two lines while every other period header is single-line, so the header band is ragged and 66px tall, breaking the visual rhythm of the period series. The period widths are also uneven (88/90/85/91), making the annual columns look irregularly spaced, and the Metric column is a touch wider than strictly needed.
critique.cause: Col 4 is 85px, giving only 64px of text space, but 'FY 2024' needs 68px. The other columns were sized ad hoc, so no consistent period width exists.

critique.good: All five headers sit on one line and the four period columns are uniform at 94px, giving a clean, regular annual series and consistent vertical rhythm. No mid-word splits.
critique.problems: The Metric column at 180px (159px text) forces four-line cells, notably the long sales-and-marketing label, pushing that row to 118px and the table to 593px. Rows stop reading as single units and the table feels loose.
critique.cause: Each period column is 94px but only needs 88–91px for its widest header/value, so roughly 25px per period column (about 100px total) is dead space that the Metric column urgently needs.

critique.good: Headers are all single-line and period columns are generously wide, so values are unambiguous and never crowded.
critique.problems: Worst readability: the Metric column at 156px (135px text) drives labels to five lines, rows up to 145px, and the table to 645px. Labels dominate the page, comparison across periods becomes tiring, and each period column carries about 30px of unused white space.
critique.cause: Metric column shrunk to 156px while all four period columns were widened to 100px, inverting the priority: the label column needs the most width, the numeric columns the least.

critique.good: All five headers stay on one line, there are no mid-word splits, and the table is the shortest at 514px. The four period columns are wide enough for every value, including $548.2M in Q1 2025, and the Metric labels wrap only at word boundaries.
critique.problems: The Metric column is necessarily narrow, so several labels run to three or four lines and the table is still tall. The annual columns are 88/90/89px, a barely visible width jitter in the historical series, and Q1 2025 has no extra width to mark it as the current period.
critique.cause: The numeric columns at their safe minimums consume 358px, leaving exactly 198px for Metric and no slack. Widening Metric or equalizing the annual columns would push at least one numeric column below its one-line minimum and reintroduce a split.

critique.good: The four period columns are all 90px, producing a clean, regular numeric grid and equal visual weight for the annual series and Q1.
critique.problems: Q1 2025 breaks $548.2M mid-word into “$548.2” and “M”, and the Free cash flow row grows from two lines to three, making the table 540px tall instead of 514px.
critique.cause: Q1 at 90px leaves only 69px of text width, one pixel short of the 70px needed for $548.2M. Metric at 196px leaves 175px of text width, just below the threshold where “trailing twelve months” still fits on one line; r1A at 198px leaves 177px and fits.

critique.good: Q1 2025 is generously wide at 98px, so its values including $548.2M stay intact, and the current period reads as a distinct endpoint.
critique.problems: FY 2023 breaks $402.7M mid-word into “$402.7” and “M”, the Free cash flow row again grows to three lines, and the annual columns become uneven at 88/89/89px while Q1 is disproportionately wide. The historical series loses rhythm.
critique.cause: FY 2023 at 89px is one pixel below the 90px minimum for $402.7M. The extra 7px given to Q1 above its 91px minimum was taken from Metric, which at 192px leaves only 171px of text and forces “trailing twelve months” to wrap.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r0C.why: All headers and numbers stay on one line and nothing breaks, but the label column is starved (~170px) so the metric names wrap to 4–5 lines (e.g. 'Net revenue / retention, / trailing twelve / months'), inflating row heights and stretching the vertical distance between a row's numbers, while the numeric columns sit wide with unused slack.

ref_equal.why: The label column is squeezed so hard that 'percentage' splits mid-word ('percentag / e of'), and labels run to 5–6 short lines ('Net revenue / retention, / trailing / twelve / months'), giving ragged, broken text next to over-wide numeric columns that need none of that space.

r1A.why: Well-proportioned: all five headers sit on one line, every number and identifier stays intact, and the ~210px label column wraps long metrics into 2–4 tidy lines without orphans or word breaks; rows read as compact units and the four year columns form an even rhythm for left-to-right comparison.

r0B.why: Essentially the same balanced solution as C with the label column a touch narrower and the year columns a touch wider; headers and figures all fit on one line, labels break at sensible points ('Customer acquisition / cost, blended'), and no column looks padded or pinched.

ref_auto.why: Labels wrap nicely and numbers are intact, but the FY 2024 column is narrower than its peers, so its header breaks into 'FY / 2024' while the other year headers stay single-line — the header band becomes uneven and one year column reads as second-class.

r0A.why: Best label wrapping of the narrow-header group (long metrics fall into two clean lines such as 'Sales and marketing expense as a / percentage of revenue'), but it repeats the flaw of a pinched FY 2024 column whose header wraps to 'FY / 2024', breaking the symmetry of the four comparable year headers.

raw.unsure: Exact pixel widths are estimated from the renders; whether B's mid-word split ('percentag/e') is a genuine width effect or an artefact of the review harness, and whether C/D's numeric columns are marginally tighter than the 68–70px content needs.

r1A.why: Headers and all figures sit on one line, numeric columns are evenly sized and the metric column is readable; however it spends a little too much width on the numeric columns (lots of empty space right of the short figures), so 'Net revenue retention, trailing twelve months' breaks into three lines with a weak orphan ('twelve months').

ref_equal.why: Metric column is squeezed to ~90px: rows run five to six lines and one label literally breaks mid-word ('percentag / e of revenue'), which is unacceptable for a publication table. Meanwhile the four numeric columns are far wider than their content needs, leaving big dead zones beside the numbers — space badly misallocated.

ref_auto.why: Metric column is generously sized so labels break sensibly (max three lines), and figures are intact, but 'FY 2024' wraps to two lines while the neighbouring year headers stay on one, breaking the parallel header series and making the header band ragged; the FY 2024 column also reads as slightly narrower than its siblings.

r0B.why: Best balance: all four period headers and every figure sit on one line, the metric column takes the remaining width and wraps into two to four tidy lines ('Net revenue retention, / trailing twelve months'), so the row-header hierarchy is clear, the year series is parallel, and the numeric columns are tight without clipping.

r0A.why: Essentially the same trade-off as C: comfortable metric column and intact figures, but 'FY 2024' is forced onto two lines, so the header row is uneven and the four year columns no longer read as an identical series; it looks near-identical to C in the render.

r0C.why: Headers and figures all on one line and the metric column is close to optimal, but the wrapping is slightly less tidy than D — first row still takes three lines and 'Sales and marketing expense as a percentage of revenue' runs to four, giving a less even row rhythm.

raw.unsure: I am estimating widths by eye, so A, D and F are within a few pixels of each other; C and E look practically identical in the renders, and I cannot be sure D's minimal numeric columns wouldn't clip a slightly wider figure or header in another rendering context.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
